correctness.rationale: Arbitrary antiderivative tests in the three coordinate variables give \(\mathbb E[y\mid x]=0\), \(\mathbb E[x+z^2\mid y]=0\), and \(\mathbb E[y\mid z]=2z-1\). Coordinate stationarity fixes \(\mathbb E[z]=1/2\) and \(\mathbb E[x]=-\mathbb E[z^2]\). Stationarity of \(y^2/2\), \(xz\), and \(yz\) gives the exact third moment, covariance, and variance identities. The deep-excursion implication follows from the nonnegative factorization \(\mathbb E[(z-1/2)^2(z+1/2)]=0\) under the hypothetical half-space restriction and invariant-support tangency. The packaged checker verifies all polynomial algebra and exact coefficients.

originality.rationale: The full foundational Sprott paper gives the exact Case N equations, its unique equilibrium, Lyapunov data, and numerical attractor plot, but no invariant-measure or stationary-moment theorem. The 2004 all-systems analytical paper and the 2005 all-systems periodic-localization paper are genuine comparison risks; complete relevant text was unavailable, so no blanket noncoverage claim is made. The accepted theorem is formulated for arbitrary compact invariant probability measures and centers on conditional expectations, a universal correlation, and a Borel-mass excursion obstruction rather than periodic-orbit localization. Eight semantic-index searches over direct and equivalent formulations returned no same-object implication.

value.rationale: Case N was introduced as a prototypical simple chaotic flow and is specifically illustrated by a numerical strange-attractor plot in the foundational paper. The accepted theorem supplies exact stationary statistics that are independent of which compact recurrent component is sampled: every non-equilibrium stationary state has the same correlation \(\sqrt{2/3}\), a fixed negative relation between central skewness and variance, and a forced excursion more than one unit below the equilibrium height. These are natural, coordinate-level invariants with direct use as exact consistency tests for numerical or experimental stationary data and as geometric constraints on any compact recurrent set supporting an invariant measure.
